title: Androgenetic alopecia (male & female)
summary: Male pattern: recession plus vertex. Female pattern: a widened parting with the frontal line kept. Topical minoxidil for both sexes, finasteride 1 mg for men, and an honest view of PRP and off-label options.

glance.think: Gradual, non-scarring thinning: frontotemporal recession and vertex in men; widening central parting or crown in women.
glance.engine: DHT (via 5α-reductase) miniaturises genetically susceptible follicles and shortens anagen.
glance.backbone: Topical minoxidil (both sexes) and oral finasteride 1 mg (men), started early and continued. Gains reverse on stopping.
glance.never_miss: Scarring alopecia (lost follicle openings, inflammation), hyperandrogenism in women, and telogen effluvium triggers (iron, thyroid).

what: **Androgenetic alopecia (AGA)** is genetically predisposed, androgen-mediated, progressive **follicular miniaturisation**.

head: Male pattern (MPHL)
Female pattern (FPHL)
rows: Mid-frontal and crown thinning with a **widened parting** (‘Christmas tree’); **frontal hairline usually preserved** (Ludwig/Sinclair)
Usually **normal**. Check for PCOS if there are acne, hirsutism or irregular periods

list: **DHT** (from testosterone via 5α-reductase) shortens anagen and miniaturises follicles in a genetically susceptible scalp.
Polygenic inheritance from **both** sides of the family.
Women with true hyperandrogenism may show a male-type pattern with acne, hirsutism and irregular periods (consider PCOS).
Gradual, **non-scarring** thinning with miniaturised hairs and **variable hair diameter**.
The pull test is usually **negative** (positive in telogen effluvium).
Psychological distress is common in both sexes.
**Bloods** if there is sudden shedding, signs of scarring, or features of hyperandrogenism or systemic disease in women: **ferritin, TFTs**, and hormones as indicated.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Acute diffuse shedding 2–3 months after a trigger; **positive pull test**
Patchy, with exclamation-mark hairs; may be diffuse
Trauma pattern; broken hairs of different lengths
Loss of follicle openings, redness, scale, pain. **Refer**

management: Check doses in the current BNF and SmPC. Off-label agents follow local dermatology advice.

list: **Topical minoxidil** 2% or 5% for **both sexes**. It must be used continuously. An **initial shed** is possible in the first weeks. Facial hair can appear if it runs onto the face. Allow about 6 months to judge the effect.

**Oral finasteride 1 mg** (men), a type II 5α-reductase inhibitor. Counsel on **sexual and mood side effects** (MHRA warning on psychiatric effects and suicidal thoughts). It is **teratogenic to a male fetus**: contraindicated in pregnancy, and women who are or may become pregnant must not handle crushed or broken tablets. Not licensed for women of childbearing potential.

management.h: Other options: overview, caution and referral

head: Option
Notes
rows: Off-label anti-androgen, especially with hyperandrogenism. Monitor potassium and BP; contraception needed. Specialist or an experienced IP within competence
Off-label, with growing evidence. Side effects: hypertrichosis, fluid retention, tachycardia. **Specialist initiation**, not a casual community start
Autologous concentrated platelets injected into the scalp. **Mixed evidence quality**, non-standard protocols, private cost. An adjunct, not a replacement

red_flags: Signs of **scarring alopecia** (lost follicle openings, inflammation, pain or itch): refer.
Rapid or patchy loss, or a positive pull test: look for another diagnosis.
Women with acne, hirsutism and irregular periods: assess for **PCOS** or hyperandrogenism.
Mood change or sexual dysfunction on finasteride: review and stop if needed (MHRA).
pearls: **Early treatment preserves more hair** than late rescue.
Stopping treatment means **gains reverse** over months, so explain this before starting.
Women: exclude scarring alopecia and reversible causes (iron, thyroid) before long-term cosmetic treatment.
Finasteride counselling must cover psychiatric and sexual side effects and pregnancy safety for partners.
PRP: avoid overselling it. Document informed expectations. Platelet disorders and anticoagulation need specialist judgement.
